processing: A clone, not a processing style: plants are propagated from cuttings and the leaf is handled like other Darjeeling, most often as black tea with a light first-flush oxidation and a fuller one later in the year.
harvest_season: Picked through the Darjeeling flushes. One estate describes herbal spring tea, chocolate and wood in summer, and a return to spring-like character in autumn.
appearance_dry: As is typical of Darjeeling clonal lots, twisted leaf in mixed green and brown, darker in summer pickings.
appearance_liquor: Typically pale gold in spring and deeper amber in summer, as with other Darjeeling.
appearance_wet: Typically a mix of green and coppery leaf, with more copper in later flushes.
taste_profile: In spring, vegetable and herbal notes that one Darjeeling grower regards as unlike its other clones; in summer, chocolate and wood.

brewing.notes: Usual Darjeeling Western-style starting point; use cooler water and a shorter steep for spring lots, and no milk.

vintage_note: Sold, when named at all, by estate, flush and year, with the clone stated on single-estate lots. As with other Darjeeling, spring tea is best drunk fresh from the current year, while summer and autumn lots hold a little longer. Unnamed clonal leaf may also end up in estate blends.
description:
B157 is one of a handful of clones behind modern Darjeeling planting, alongside P312 and AV2. It is a plant selection rather than a finished tea, so you will mostly meet it as a line on an estate's product page.

As a clone, every plant is grown from cuttings of one selected bush, so the character is more repeatable than in seed-grown gardens. The leaf then goes through whichever process the estate chooses, usually black tea in the Darjeeling manner.

Gopaldhara, which grows it, describes distinctly vegetable and herbal spring tea, then chocolate and wood in summer, with autumn tea that keeps something of spring. Treat this as a grower's description of its own garden. Terroir and processing count too. Brew it as you would any Darjeeling, gently in spring.

Look for the estate, flush and year, because the clone name alone tells you little. Tasting a B157 and a P312 from one garden and one season is the clearest way to learn what a clone contributes.
history: B157 is documented as one of the cultivars used in newer Darjeeling plantings, which moved from the original China seed stock towards saplings from selected clones adapted to the district. The name points to the Bannockburn garden, but a reliable record of its selection and release date is hard to come by, so little more can be said about its origin.
